--- title: "Image classification with neural networks" subtitle: "STA5073Z Data Science for Industry: Assignment 2" author: - Corey Webb - Shirley Knight - Jess Prevost bibliography: dsfi_a2.bib execute: warning: false message: false echo: false --- ## Introduction Handwriting styles vary between individuals and develop over years of practice, making handwriting a distinctive yet subtle biometric trait. Writer identification from handwritten samples has practical applications in forensic document examination, authorship attribution, and biometric authentication [@Abushahla2026]. Advances in machine learning enable models to learn discriminative features directly from raw images, providing an opportunity to investigate how effectively different architectures capture writer-specific characteristics. This report uses a dataset of 25,000 images of handwritten digits (0-4), contributed by 20 writers over 5 sessions, with 50 samples per digit, writer and session. The dataset enables investigation of within-session and between-session variation, while its limited number of writers and structured sampling inform the experimental design and evaluation strategy. Convolutional neural networks (CNNs) are a class of neural networks designed to hierarchically learn spatial features from image data [@Reza2026; @Yamashita2018]. Convolutional layers apply filters to learn local patterns such as stroke edges and curves; pooling layers summarise these features into lower-dimensional representations, retaining the most important information while reducing sensitivity to small positional changes. The extracted features are subsequently passed to fully connected layers, which produce predictions over the possible writer classes, with the final layer outputting a probability distribution across the classes. In this application, the CNN is trained to answer: which writer produced this image? Siamese neural networks (SNNs) reframe this question. Rather than assigning an image to a writer, a SNN takes two images and asks: were these written by the same person? Both images are processed by identical CNN subnetworks with shared weights, producing embeddings that represent learned visual characteristics. The distance between the embeddings provides a measure of the similarity between the two samples. The network is trained to encourage same-writer images to have embeddings close together and push different-writer embeddings further apart, using a contrastive loss function. A threshold on the embedding distance then converts it into a binary classification of same or different [@He2025]. Introduced originally for signature verification [@Bromley1993] and subsequently applied to other recognition tasks, SNNs have demonstrated potential across a range of applications, including signature identification [@herman_2026] and malware image classification [@Hsiao_2019]. Their ability to learn pairwise similarities makes them well-suited to handwriting verification. Moreover, their effectiveness in one-shot learning has been demonstrated in malware image classification, where similarity-based learning enables classification with limited training data [@Hsiao_2019]. In the context of handwriting verification, evaluating performance on writers excluded from training provides a means of assessing the model's ability to generalise to unseen writers. This report compares CNN-based writer identification and SNN-based writer verification to investigate how effectively each approach distinguishes individual writing styles in handwritten digit images. It explores the dataset, evaluates both architectures, and compares their performance across hyperparameter configurations, writing sessions, and digit classes, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations. ## Exploratory data analysis The provided dataset consists of a four-dimensional array containing 25,000 images of handwritten digits, along with associated metadata. Each image has a resolution of 28 x 28 pixels and contains a single channel representing greyscale intensity. The five digits from 0 - 4 were each written 50 times by 20 different individuals during each of the five independent sessions. The array contains no missing values, indicating all images and associated metadata were complete. Pixel values ranged from 0, indicating a blank background, to 255, representing a pixel with maximal intensity. Variation arose between individuals in several ways (@fig-inter-ind_var), including differences in digit size, particularly for the digit '0'. As shown in (@fig-inter-ind_var), individuals 3 and 12 had much smaller '0's than individuals 1, 10, and 16. The angle and curvature of strokes also varied. For example, the vertical stroke in digit '1' was straight for individual 1, more curved for individual 3 and straight but more diagonal for individual 10. Similarly, the diagonal and vertical strokes in digit '4' varied in angle and curvature across individuals. The digit '0' also tilted in different directions for individuals 10 and 12 compared to 1,3, and 16 (@fig-inter-ind_var). Although inter-individual variation was more pronounced, variation was still observed within individuals, both across sessions (@fig-within-ind-var) and within a given session (@fig-within-ind-var-single-session). Repeated samples of a given digit by the same individual tended to be similar in size. However, some variation once again arose in the angle and curvature of strokes, such as the top-right corner of the digit '0' and the angle of the bottom horizontal stroke of the digit '2' (@fig-within-ind-var). Intra-individual variation was more apparent across different sessions than within the same session. For individual 16, the bottom stroke of the digit '2' was more consistent across samples in the same session than across different sessions. Within the same individual and session, there was more variation in pixel intensity, as illustrated by the bottom horizontal stroke of the digit '1' (@fig-within-ind-var-single-session). There are several visible limitations to the simulated handwritten digit data. First, some digits contain unusually straight lines and sharp angles in digits where these are unlikely to occur in natural handwriting. An example is the top-right corner of the digit '0' for individual 10 (@fig-inter-ind_var). Second, line continuity is sometimes interrupted, as seen in the gaps in the digit '2' across sessions 3, 4 and 5 for individual 16 (@fig-within-ind-var) and in all selected samples for digit '2' from session 1 (@fig-within-ind-var-single-session). Furthermore, the simulated data does not capture variation in stroke thickness that would arise from variable pressure during real-world writing. There is also limited variation in digit style; for example, the digit '1' can be written as a single vertical line, which is not represented in the simulated data. In some cases, the simulated data also appears unrealistic. For instance, individual 3's digit '1' which closely resembles a '2', making it difficult to identify the intended digit. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Handwritten digits for four randomly selected individuals indicating inter-individual variability within a single session (Session 1, Samples 1).](index_files/figure-html/fig-inter-ind_var-1.png){#fig-inter-ind_var width=480} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Handwritten digits for a single randomly selected individual (Person 16) from five different sessions (all Sample 1) indicating within-individual variability across sessions.](index_files/figure-html/fig-within-ind-var-1.png){#fig-within-ind-var width=480} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Handwritten digits for a single randomly selected individual (Person 16) from five random samples within a single session (Session 1) indicating within-individual variability within a session](index_files/figure-html/fig-within-ind-var-single-session-1.png){#fig-within-ind-var-single-session width=480} ::: ::: ## Train, validation and test strategy The Siamese network and the CNN used different data-splitting strategies to reflect their distinct tasks: the Siamese network was split by writer, while CNN was split by session. However, the proportions were kept consistent for both models: 60% for training, 20% for validation, and 20% for testing. The Siamese network dataset was split at the writer level to ensure that no writer appeared in more than one set. A random image-level split was avoided, as this would allow the same writer to appear in both training and test sets, potentially producing an overly optimistic estimate of the model's generalisability. Testing on unseen writers provides a more meaningful assessment of the model's ability to verify handwriting from individuals not encountered during training. This evaluation reflects how the model would perform in a real-world setting; for example, verifying whether two documents were written by the same previously unseen individual. Image pairs were constructed independently within each split to prevent images from overlapping across datasets. A key limitation of this strategy is the small number of writers in this dataset. With only 20 writers in total, the split allocates just four writers each to the validation and test sets, making performance estimates noisy and sensitive to which writers were assigned to each set. Furthermore, the decision threshold was selected by maximising balanced accuracy on the validation set and is therefore optimised for those four specific writers, which may limit its generalisability to other unseen writers. The CNN dataset was split at the session-level. Since the task was writer-identification, the model had to be trained on images from all writers and evaluated on its performance on the sessions held out from training. This evaluation reflects the scenario of: given a set of handwritten images from a new session, how accurately can the model identify the writer? A limitation of this strategy is the small number of available sessions, with three used for training, one for validation and one for testing. For both models, the test set was kept independent and used only for final evaluation, providing an unbiased assessment of model performance on the held-out data. ## Writer identification with a CNN The prediction task is closed-set writer identification: given a single 28 x 28 image of a digit, the model predicts which of the 20 writers produced it. The CNN follows the structure of the lecture example (@tbl-cnn-structure). It was trained on sessions 1-3, with session 4 used for validation and to decide when to stop training. Session 5 was held out as the test set, ensuring that all test images come from a session not seen during training. The analysis was conducted in R version 4.6.1 [@R]. Both CNNs and Siamese networks were fitted using the Keras framework via the *keras3* R package [@keras3] using the TensorFlow backend [@tensorflow]. The tidyverse package [@tidyverse] was utilised throughout the analysis for data manipulation and plotting using *ggplot2.* ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ### Model structure ::: {#tbl-cnn-structure .cell tbl-cap='Layers of the CNN used for writer identification, with the shape of each layer\'s output and its number of trainable parameters.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Layer (type) |Output shape | Parameters| |:----------------------------|:------------------|----------:| |input_layer (InputLayer) |(None, 28, 28, 1) | 0| |conv2d (Conv2D) |(None, 26, 26, 16) | 160| |activation (Activation) |(None, 26, 26, 16) | 0| |dropout (Dropout) |(None, 26, 26, 16) | 0| |conv2d_1 (Conv2D) |(None, 24, 24, 16) | 2320| |max_pooling2d (MaxPooling2D) |(None, 12, 12, 16) | 0| |flatten (Flatten) |(None, 2304) | 0| |dense (Dense) |(None, 20) | 46100| |Total | | 48580| ::: ::: ### Training ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Accuracy of the CNN after each epoch on the training sessions (1-3) and the validation session (4). Training stopped once validation accuracy had not improved for 10 epochs.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cnn-history-1.png){#fig-cnn-history width=576} ::: ::: ### Writer identification performance #### What the evaluation measures capture In real-world terms, accuracy represents the proportion of handwritten digit images correctly attributed to the writer, assuming the writer is one of the 20 enrolled individuals and the digit was written in a session not used for training. A system based on this model would correctly identify the writer from a single digit approximately half the time. However, this measure says nothing about individuals outside the 20 enrolled writers, as the model would still assign images to one of them. Accuracy by digit indicates which digits may contain more writer-specific information, while the confusion matrix shows which writers are most frequently mistaken for one another. This is particularly relevant when an incorrect attribution has consequences for the person identified. #### Results of the basic CNN On the test session, the CNN named the correct writer for 50.1% of images (@tbl-cnn-accuracy), compared with 5% expected baseline (random guessing). Accuracy differed by digit (@tbl-cnn-by-digit): it was highest for digit 2 (59.1%) and lowest for digit 0 (44.5%). Each digit has 1000 test images from the single session that was not used in training or validation. #### Error analysis Errors were concentrated in particular writers (@tbl-cnn-confusion). Three writers were identified in at least 95% of their images, whereas writers 5, 10, and 13 were identified in at most 5% of theirs; for example, 243 of the 250 images from writer 10 were attributed to writer 2. #### Overfitting The CNN overfits to the training sessions (@fig-cnn-history). Validation accuracy came within two percentage points of its maximum (57.3%) by epoch 11 and then stayed flat, while training accuracy kept rising to 99.9% by the end of training at epoch 30. The later epochs therefore appear to have fitted features of the training sessions that did not generalise to a new session. Validation accuracy did not fall, so the additional training gave no benefit. For this reason, the hyperparameter search uses the earliest epoch whose validation accuracy was within one standard error of the best observed value, rather than continuing training unnecessarily. ::: {#tbl-cnn-accuracy .cell tbl-cap='Overall writer identification accuracy of the CNN on the validation session (used for early stopping) and on the untouched test session.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Set | Images| Accuracy (%)| |:----------------------|------:|------------:| |Validation (session 4) | 5000| 57.3| |Test (session 5) | 5000| 50.1| ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-cnn-by-digit .cell tbl-cap='Writer identification accuracy of the CNN on the test session for each digit, from most to least accurate.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Digit | Images| Accuracy (%)| |:-----|------:|------------:| |2 | 1000| 59.1| |1 | 1000| 51.0| |4 | 1000| 49.5| |3 | 1000| 46.4| |0 | 1000| 44.5| ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-cnn-confusion .cell tbl-cap='Confusion matrix of the CNN on the test session. Each row is the true writer (250 test images each) and each column the writer the CNN predicted, so reading across a row shows where that writer\'s images went. The layer structure and batch size were fixed. Each combination was evaluated using four-fold cross-validation (CV) over sessions 1-4, with one session held out per fold; session 5 was not used. Validation accuracy was recorded after each epoch and the number of epochs was set to the earliest epoch within one standard error (SE) of the best observed validation accuracy to help guard against overfitting. A coarse grid search was followed by a refined grid search around its best-performing region. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: #### Coarse grid ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Coarse grid search: best cross-validated accuracy of each combination of learning rate, dropout rate and number of filters (4-fold cross-validation over sessions 1-4).](index_files/figure-html/fig-cnn-hpo-coarse-1.png){#fig-cnn-hpo-coarse width=672} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-cnn-hpo-coarse .cell tbl-cap='The five combinations with the highest cross-validated (CV) accuracy in the coarse grid search (27 combinations). The one-SE epoch is the earliest epoch whose CV accuracy is within one standard error of the best epoch.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} | Learning rate| Dropout rate| Filters| Best CV accuracy (%)| Standard error (%)| Best epoch| One-SE epoch| CV accuracy at one-SE epoch (%)| |-------------:|------------:|-------:|--------------------:|------------------:|----------:|------------:|-------------------------------:| | 0.0001| 0.5| 32| 57.6| 2.2| 11| 4| 55.9| | 0.0001| 0.5| 16| 57.6| 2.0| 14| 7| 55.8| | 0.0001| 0.2| 16| 57.4| 1.4| 16| 7| 56.0| | 0.0001| 0.5| 8| 57.3| 1.7| 19| 10| 55.9| | 0.001| 0.5| 32| 57.2| 2.4| 1| 1| 57.2| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Learning rate had the largest effect on CV accuracy (@fig-cnn-hpo-coarse): averaged over the other two hyperparameters, CV accuracy fell from 57.0% at a learning rate of 0.0001 to 52.6% at 0.01. Dropout had a smaller effect (54.8% with no dropout, 55.7% at 0.5), while the number of filters had little effect (55.0% to 55.5%). The best-performing learning rate and dropout rate were both at the edge of the coarse grid (@tbl-cnn-hpo-coarse), so the refined grid extended the ranges of both hyperparameters and fixed the number of filters at 16. Due to the lower learning rate, the refined grid used 40 epochs instead of 20. #### Refined grid ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Refined grid search: best cross-validated accuracy for lower learning rates and higher dropout rates, with the number of filters fixed at 16.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cnn-hpo-refined-1.png){#fig-cnn-hpo-refined width=432} ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-cnn-hpo-refined .cell tbl-cap='The five combinations with the highest cross-validated (CV) accuracy in the refined grid search (9 combinations).'} ::: {.cell-output-display} | Learning rate| Dropout rate| Filters| Best CV accuracy (%)| Standard error (%)| Best epoch| One-SE epoch| CV accuracy at one-SE epoch (%)| |-------------:|------------:|-------:|--------------------:|------------------:|----------:|------------:|-------------------------------:| | 0.0001| 0.8| 16| 58.6| 2.0| 32| 11| 57.0| | 0.0001| 0.7| 16| 58.4| 2.1| 14| 9| 56.8| | 0.0003| 0.8| 16| 58.1| 1.9| 12| 5| 56.3| | 0.00003| 0.7| 16| 58.0| 2.1| 38| 23| 55.8| | 0.0003| 0.7| 16| 57.9| 1.4| 14| 5| 56.5| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: The refined grid showed little variation in CV accuracy (@fig-cnn-hpo-refined): its nine combinations ranged only from 57.6% to 58.6%, a range smaller than the standard error of a single combination (approximately 2 percentage points). This suggested the search had reached a plateau. #### Selected model and sensitivity The hyperparameter combination with the highest CV accuracy had a learning rate of 0.0001, a dropout rate of 0.8 and 16 filters (@tbl-cnn-hpo-refined). Its CV accuracy peaked at epoch 32 (58.6%) but was within one SE of that from epoch 11 (57.0%), so 11 epochs were used (@fig-cnn-hpo-epochs). Across both grids, CV accuracy ranged from 51.1% to 58.6%. Writer identification accuracy was therefore moderately sensitive to the learning rate, which accounted for most of this variation, but showed little sensitivity to dropout rate and number of filters across the values tested. No hyperparameter combination resulted in substantial improvement in model performance, with the hyperparameter-tuned model identifying the correct writer only around 55% of the time. Although this is better than random guessing, the model remains relatively unsuitable for the task. Whether this is due to the model architecture or the limited amount of data (only five sessions) is unclear. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Cross-validated accuracy (points) with one standard error either side (bars) after each epoch for the selected hyperparameters. The dashed line marks the best epoch and the solid line the one-SE epoch that was used.](index_files/figure-html/fig-cnn-hpo-epochs-1.png){#fig-cnn-hpo-epochs width=576} ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {#tbl-cnn-hpo-test .cell tbl-cap='Writer identification accuracy of the tuned CNN on the test session (session 5), overall and for each digit. The test session played no part in choosing the hyperparameters.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} |Digit | Images| Accuracy (%)| |:----------|------:|------------:| |2 | 1000| 56.5| |4 | 1000| 53.4| |3 | 1000| 52.9| |1 | 1000| 51.8| |0 | 1000| 51.4| |All digits | 5000| 53.2| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Writer identification accuracy on the test session for each writer, for the basic CNN and the tuned CNN, ordered from most to least accurately identified by the tuned CNN. Dashed blue line: overall accuracy of the tuned CNN. Dotted orange line: overall accuracy of the basic CNN. Grey line: accuracy expected from random guessing (5%).](index_files/figure-html/fig-cnn-hpo-writer-1.png){#fig-cnn-hpo-writer width=672} ::: ::: Retrained on sessions 1-4 with the selected hyperparameters, the CNN identified the writer correctly for 53.2% of test images (@tbl-cnn-hpo-test), compared with 50.1% for the untuned model. These results are not directly comparable, because the tuned model was also trained on one additional session. Test accuracy was lower than the CV estimate (57.0%), which is expected because the CV estimate was also used to select the hyperparameters [@varma_2006] and because sessions may differ in difficulty. Accuracy across digits was more consistent than for the untuned model, ranging from 51.4% to 56.5%. By writer (@fig-cnn-hpo-writer), the tuned model was more accurate than the basic model for 10 writers and less accurate for 7; writers 5 and 13 were almost never correctly identified by either model. ## Writer verification with a Siamese network A Siamese neural network was trained on the handwriting images and evaluated to assess how accurately it could capture whether two digits were written by the same writer. We controlled for digit identity by constructing pairs consisting of the same digits. Therefore, a positive pair for this network consisted of two different images of the same digit written by the same person, and a negative pair contained two images of the same digit but by different writers. Examples of pairs from the training and validation datasets are shown in @fig-pairs. We employed a balanced pair sampling approach with half of the pairs being positive and the remaining half negative to ensure the Siamese network learned effectively [@chopra_2005]. ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Example training and validation pairs. Top row: training pairs (same writer left, different writer right). Bottom row: validation pairs (same writer left, different writer right).](index_files/figure-html/fig-pairs-1.png){#fig-pairs width=672} ::: ::: We used contrastive loss, introduced by @hadsell_2006, to train the Siamese network. This loss function was chosen over triplet loss because our interest is in distinguishing same-writer from different-writer pairs, rather than learning a relative ranking of dissimilarity between triplets. Additionally, this is a simple binary verification task and the dataset is relatively small. Contrastive loss may therefore be particularly suitable for this setting, given evidence that it can converge faster than triplet loss [@herman_2026]. The contrastive loss for a pair is: $$ L = yD^2 + (1-y)\max(0,m-D)^2 $$ where $y$ is a binary label with $y = 1$ for a positive pair (i.e., the same writer and same digit) and $D$ is the Euclidean distance between the embeddings. The hyperparameter $m$ defines the margin: similar pairs incur near-zero loss when their embeddings are close ($d$ is small), while dissimilar pairs incur zero loss only if their distance is at least $m$. This encourages the network to minimise distances between embeddings from the same writer and maximise distances between embeddings from different writers, up to the margin [@Elaraby_2023]. The margin for the initial Siamese network was set as 1, but was optimised in a hyperparameter search in [Hyperparameter optimisation](#hyperparameter-optimisation). The data were split into 60% training, 20% validation, and 20% test sets. Data were grouped by writer, with different writers assigned to each set, to ensure that the network learnt to recognise similarities in writing style without exposure to the validation and test writers during training. This allowed the model's generalisability to unseen writers to be tested. However, since there were only 20 writers, this split meant that only 4 writers were included in each of the validation and test sets. This is a significant limitation and is discussed further in [Train, validation and test strategy](#train-validation-and-test-strategy). The shared CNN encoder consisted of two convolutional layers with 16 and 32 filters, respectively, each using a filter size of 3 and a ReLU activation function to introduce non-linearity. A max pooling layer with a pool size and stride of 2 was placed between these convolutional layers. The convolutional layers learn local image features while max pooling reduces the spatial dimensions of the feature maps. The last two layers were a global average pooling layer which converts the feature maps into a vector and a dense layer mapping the vector to a 16-dimensional embedding. A relatively simple encoder is used since the input images are low-resolution and contain features such as curves and strokes that the network can learn from these images. In the Siamese model, pairs of images are supplied to the encoder to produce their embeddings and then the Euclidean distance between each pair is calculated. The model was compiled using the Adam optimiser and used the above contrastive loss function which was calculated using the Euclidean distances and a margin of one, and averaged for every batch. Epoch was set to 5 and batch size to 64. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: We compared the balanced accuracy for same and different digit pairs from the validation set at different Euclidean distance thresholds, and chose the threshold which maximised the balanced accuracy. The different thresholds tested were all the actual distances between the validation pairs. The selected threshold was 0.44 giving a validation balanced accuracy of 78.73%. The generalisability of our model was evaluated by predicting on unseen writers' digit image-pairs in the test set and calculating the balanced accuracy. Balanced accuracy was also calculated by digit to assess how performance varied for different digits (@tbl-snn-test-digits) and calculated separately for pairs in the same and different sessions to how session changes affects performance (@tbl-snn-test-sessions). We did not specify how many of each digit to be used nor whether images should be from the same or different sessions when creating pairs of images. Thus, the number of pairs of images of each digit, and whether the pair was from the same session or not were random with ratios related to the proportion images of each digit (1:1:1:1:1; @tbl-snn-test-digits) and the proportion of images in the same and different sessions in the test set (1:4; @tbl-snn-test-sessions). Examples of pairs from the test batch with predicted and true values are shown in @fig-test-results. ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {#tbl-snn-test-digits .cell tbl-cap='Balanced accuracy for Siamese neural network predictions on pairs of images in the test set including a breakdown of balanced accuracy by digit ordered from highest to lowest balanced accuracy.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} | Digit| Image pairs| Test balanced accuracy (%)| |----------:|-----------:|--------------------------:| | 4| 986| 86.5| | 3| 1020| 85.2| | 1| 980| 82.6| | 0| 1022| 82.3| | 2| 992| 76.4| | All digits| 5000| 82.6| ::: ::: ::: {#tbl-snn-test-sessions .cell tbl-cap='Balanced accuracy for Siamese neural network predictions on pairs of images in the test set including a breakdown of balanced accuracy for digits in the same and in different sessions.'} ::: {.cell-output-display} | Session| Image pairs| Test balanced accuracy (%)| |-----------------:|-----------:|--------------------------:| | Same session| 1003| 94.2| | Different session| 3997| 79.6| | All sessions| 5000| 82.6| ::: ::: ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![Sample test pairs with true label, predicted label, and distance score. Green border = correct prediction, red = incorrect.](index_files/figure-html/fig-test-results-1.png){#fig-test-results width=672} ::: ::: ### Siamese network hyperparameter search For the Siamese neural network, the margin $m$, learning rate, and batch size were tuned using a grid search, while the CNN encoder architecture and number of epochs were fixed. For each hyperparameter combination, the validation balanced accuracy was calculated at different thresholds, and the threshold that maximised balanced accuracy was selected. However, using the same validation dataset to select the threshold and evaluate balanced accuracy is a limitation. Ideally, the validation data would be divided into two sets, with one used to calculate the threshold from and the other to evaluate balanced accuracy at that threshold. However, because the validation pairs were constructed from only four writers, this dataset was too small to split meaningfully. As with the CNN hyperparameter tuning, a coarse grid search using 36 combinations of hyperparameters (@fig-snn-hpo-coarse) was followed by a refined grid search involving 9 combinations around the best-performing region in the coarse grid (@fig-snn-hpo-refined). ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: ::: {.cell} ::: Once again, learning rate had the largest effect on balanced accuracy (@fig-snn-hpo-coarse). Averaged across the other two hyperparameters, balanced accuracy fell from 79.14% at a learning rate of 0.01 to 73.51% at 0.0001. Both the margin (76.02% at $m = 2$ up to 78.31% at $m = 0.5$) and the batch size (75.39% at a batch size of 128, compared with 78.2% at 32) had smaller effects on balanced accuracy. The best-performing learning rate and margin were at the edge of the coarse grid (@fig-snn-hpo-coarse), so the refined grid extended the ranges of both variables and fixed the batch size at 32 (@fig-snn-hpo-refined). Their accuracy metrics are not directly comparable. Nevertheless, both tuned models substantially outperformed what would be expected by chance: SNN achieved a test balanced accuracy of 0.8187029 (compared with 50% baseline for binary verification of same- vs different-writer) and the CNN a test accuracy of 53.2% (compared with a 5% baseline for classifying one out of 20 writers). These results indicate that both networks learned useful writer-related features for their respective tasks. ::: {.cell} ::: At the digit level, the networks had varied performance. The tuned CNN's identification accuracy ranged from 51.4% for digit 0 to 56.5% for digit 2 (@tbl-cnn-hpo-test). In comparison, the tuned SNN's balanced accuracy ranged from 78.7% for digit 2 % to 84.9% for digit 3 (@tbl-snn-hpo-test-digits). Notably, digit 2 had the highest identification accuracy for the CNN but the lowest balanced accuracy for the SNN. Although the results may initially appear contradictory, they suggest that the usefulness of a digit depends on the nature of the task being performed. Digits achieving a high identification accuracy (CNN) and low balanced accuracy (SNN) (e.g., digit '2') means that 2 can help to distinguish among the writers represented in the training data, but that the same digit does not provide equally useful information in verifying whether two samples were written by the same writer Conversely, digits with high balanced accuracy (SNN) and low accuracy (CNN) may provide useful evidence for distinguishing same-writer from different-writer pairs, without being sufficiently distinctive to identify a particular writer from the 20 known writers. For example, digit 0 may exhibit this pattern, while digits 3 and 4 achieved mid-to-high performance across both metrics which may show that it serves usefulness in both tasks. However, it is important to note that these interpretations are suggestive rather than definitive, as these models were evaluated using different data splits and under different generalisation settings. ::: {.cell} ::: Session-related performance was assessed using the SNN, by comparing performance for pairs drawn from the same sessions with pairs from different sessions. This was not possible for the CNN, because its session-level split was designed to perform writer identification on held-out sessions. The SNN achieved higher balanced accuracy for same-session pairs than for different-session pairs (90.8% versus 79.6%). This result is consistent with our expectation that writer variation across sessions makes verification more difficult. However, this difference alone does not establish which sources of variation were responsible (e.g., natural writer variation, different writing materials). Performance also varied considerably across writers in the CNN evaluation. The model identified writers 7 & 18 with near-perfect accuracy, whereas it nearly always misclassified samples from writers 5 & 13. This suggests that some writers had handwriting that was far more distinguishable than the others. Because the SNN datasets were split by writer, we cannot compare the performance with respect to individual writers as directly, although we note that writers 5 & 13 happened to be in the validation set used for HP tuning, which may explain why validation accuracy was lower than test accuracy (78.54% versus 81.87. The higher test result may reflect differences in the difficulty of the validation and test writers, as well as sampling variability, rather than a general improvement in performance on unseen writers. Finally, hyperparameter tuning indicated moderate sensitivity for both models to the learning rate. For the CNN, tuning the other hyperparameters offered no substantial additional improvements in performance, whereas a smaller batch size tended to improve the SNN's balanced accuracy. Overall, the results demonstrate both networks can learn useful features from handwritten images for writer identification and writer verification, while also highlighting the effects of digit choice, session variation, writer-specific differences, and evaluation design on measured performance. ## Conclusion ## Plagiarism declaration {.unnumbered} ## AI use statement {.unnumbered}
